Data visualization guide

How McKesson Workforce Innovation turns workforce data into charts that lead to decisions.

Version 0.2 (pilot)September 2026All example data is synthetic
McKesson Data Visualization GuideOverview1

Overview

How to use this guide

One set of rules, three ways in. The guide teaches the thinking; the starter kit makes the right answer the easy one in every tool we use.

Every chart we make should do one job: answer a business question so clearly that the reader knows what to do next. The rules here are written to be checked, by a reviewer or by an agent, before a chart leaves the team.

Inspired by the structure of a leading consulting firm's public data-visualization guide, rebuilt for McKesson's brand and for the work of Workforce Innovation.

Consultants and analysts

Decks, reports, workbooks

Read Fundamentals once, then use the chart pages as you build. Keep the cheat sheet next to you.

  • PowerPoint template and starter deck
  • Excel chart workbook with the palette
  • One-page cheat sheet and chart chooser
  • Power BI report theme

Developers and data scientists

Python, HTML, R, Power BI

Each chart page links to tested code. Themes are generated from one token file, so every tool matches.

  • mckviz for matplotlib and Plotly
  • CSS variables, Plotly and Vega-Lite themes
  • theme_mck() for ggplot2
  • mv.lint(fig) to check a chart

Coding agents

Claude, Copilot and others

Agents read AGENTS.md automatically in this repo. For other repos, copy one self-contained rules file.

  • AGENTS.md: workflow and rules
  • mck-chart skill: question to QA
  • dist/agents/mck-viz-rules.md
  • Cookbook pages with runnable snippets

The five steps behind every chart

1 Question. Write the question the chart answers in one sentence.

2 Chart. Pick the chart from the question type, not from habit.

3 Build. Grey first, then color only what the headline names.

4 Headline. Compute the finding, then write it as a sentence.

5 QA. Run the checklist and look at the rendered chart.

Fundamentals

Start with the question, not the chart

A chart is finished when a reader can say what it means and what to do about it, without you in the room.

Before you open a tool, write the question in one sentence: "Where is attrition concentrated?", not "show attrition".

Then pick the mode. Explanatory charts prove a finding, for decks and reports (the default). Exploratory views let readers find answers, for dashboards. Both follow the same rules.

Both charts here are accurate; only one is useful in a meeting.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals4

Fundamentals

How readers read a chart

Readers move through a chart in three steps. Design for each one, in order.

1 Perceive

In the first second the eye takes in shape, length and color before reading a word. Make the thing that matters the thing that stands out: one color against grey.

2 Interpret

Next the reader looks for meaning: headline, labels, units, benchmarks. The headline should confirm what they just saw, or sharpen it.

3 Act

Finally they ask "so what?". A callout that sizes the implication turns a finding into a decision.

Step 1 · Perceive

Two bars stand out

No words yet. Grey context and blue focus already tell the reader where to look.

Step 2 · Interpret

Labels give it meaning

Names, values and a labelled benchmark show the two families sit well above 19.9%.

Step 3 · Act

The callout sizes the prize

Together they hold 58% of headcount but 73% of voluntary exits: a retention plan for two families moves the enterprise number.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals5

Fundamentals

Anatomy of a chart

Every McKesson chart has the same four layers, top to bottom: headline, subtitle, chart, and footnote with source.

The headline and subtitle do different jobs. The headline is editorial: it states the finding. The subtitle is neutral: metric, unit, scope and period.

Inside the chart, everything is labelled in place, so the reader never has to match colors to a legend.

All four layers share one left edge. In HTML they are page text; the chart library draws only the data.

  1. 1Insight headlineA full sentence with the number. At most two lines, no final period.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, unit, scope and period. No opinions.
  3. 3Direct labelsSeries named at the line end, in the series color. No legend.
  4. 4Focus and contextThe series the headline is about is blue; the comparison is grey.
  5. 5Forecast markedA shaded period and dashed lines separate estimates from actuals.
  6. 6Range, not a pointForecasts show their uncertainty.
  7. 7The point, annotatedThe gap the headline quotes, labelled where it is.
  8. 8Light scaffoldingFew, light gridlines; units live in the subtitle.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceDefinitions, system, as-of date, population.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals6

Fundamentals

Write the headline last, from the numbers

The headline is the most-read text on the page. It should be the finding, not the topic.

The formula

Who or what + verb + number + so what.

Before you keep it

  • Recompute every number, "all", "most" and "n of m" from the data
  • The blue in the chart is what the headline names
  • Two lines at most; no final period

If you can't write a headline, you don't have a finding yet: you have a chart.

Label
Attrition by job family · names the topic; says nothing
Vague
Attrition varies across job families · true of every chart ever made
Opinion
Attrition is out of control in the frontline · a claim the chart can't support
Insight
Two frontline job families lose about 1 in 4 people a year, well above the 19.9% enterprise rate
Insight + action
Two frontline families account for 73% of voluntary exits; retention there moves the enterprise rate
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals7

Fundamentals

Grey first, then color the point

Color is for meaning, never decoration. Start with every mark in grey, then color only what the headline names.

Highlight at most two items. When everything is highlighted, nothing is.

Echo the highlight in the text: bold the matching category label, and set callouts in the color of the mark they describe.

Orange means "worse". Keep it for negatives: below target, shrinking, a shortfall. Never use it as a plain highlight; readers take it as a warning.

Pattern 1 · Default

Focus

All grey; the items the headline names in blue.

Pattern 2

Uniform + accent

One series in light blue; the single exception in navy.

Pattern 3

Focus + accent

Grey context, a blue group, one navy exception. Use sparingly.

Color roles

Context · everything the reader should see but not focus on#B4B0A5
Focus · what the headline names#005A8C
Accent · the one exception that must pop (navy, not orange)#143359
Light blue · the series when navy marks the exception#66C4FF
Orange · only when it means worse: below target, shrinking, a shortfall#EF8200
Total and benchmark · totals, targets, reference lines#143359
Context light · de-emphasized fills in stacks and areas#DEDBD1
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals8

Fundamentals

Three palettes, three jobs

Pick the palette from what the color encodes.

Categories

Only when categories must be told apart. At most six, always in the same order, so "Full-time" is the same blue on every slide.

One measure, light to dark

For heat tables and choropleths of a single measure. Darker means more.

Gap to a benchmark

For values centered on zero or a target. Orange below, blue above, a neutral middle.

Text on a fill switches between white and navy, whichever contrasts more (mv.text_on).

Categorical

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals9

Fundamentals

Type and proportion

One typeface, Libre Franklin, in a few fixed roles. Type should frame the data, not compete with it.

The headline is the largest text on the chart but the data is the largest thing. If the headline is the first thing you notice from across the room, it is too heavy.

  • Nothing below 9 pt on slides, 11 px on screens
  • Sentence case everywhere; no all-caps headlines
  • Headline, subtitle, key, footnote and source share one left edge
  • Big numbers use the light weight

Libre Franklin is open source (SIL OFL). Set-up for Office, the web and Power BI is in the Toolkit.

RoleSampleWeightSlideScreen
HeadlineAttrition is concentrated in two job familiesBold24 pt22 px
SubtitleVoluntary attrition, FY26 (%)Regular14 pt15 px
Data labels27.4%Medium12 pt13 px
Axis and category labelsPharmacy TechnicianRegular11 pt12 px
CalloutsHiring freeze, Q2Regular12 pt13 px
Footnote and sourceSource: Workday HCM, as of 31 Mar 2026Light9 pt11 px
Big number75%Light54 pt56 px

Proportion on a 16:9 slide

Margins of about 0.5 in. The chart takes at least 60% of the slide height. One message per chart, at most two charts per slide; the slide title is the headline.

Proportion on a screen

The chart card sits on a quiet background with generous padding. Headline about 1.4× the subtitle. On phones, swap end labels for a top key and let wide exhibits scroll sideways rather than shrink.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals10

Fundamentals

Label directly, delete the rest

Every element must earn its place. If removing it loses nothing, remove it.

  1. Replace the label-style title with an insight headline
  2. Sort by value, not alphabet
  3. Turn long-named columns into horizontal bars
  4. Grey everything, then color the point
  5. Label values in place; delete the value axis, gridlines and tick marks
  6. Delete the legend, borders and background fill
  7. Add the benchmark, labelled where it sits
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals11

Fundamentals

Honest scales

A chart can be accurate in every number and still mislead. These four rules prevent the common ways.

Bars start at zero. If the differences only show on a narrow range, change the chart, not the axis.

No dual axes. Two scales let you make any two lines cross wherever you like.

Bubble area, not diameter, is proportional to value.

Pies take five slices at most, and sum to 100%.

The one exception: a waterfall bridging two large totals may break its axis, if the break is drawn and footnoted.

Truncated bars

✕Try to avoidAn axis from 65 turns a 4% difference into a 33% one.
✓RecommendedA dot plot compares position, so the range can be narrow.

Dual axes

✕Try to avoidThe crossing point is an artifact of two chosen scales.
✓RecommendedTwo aligned charts share the time axis.

Bubble size

✕Try to avoidSized by diameter, 900 looks 81× bigger than 100.
✓RecommendedSized by area, 900 is 9× bigger, as it should be.

Too many slices

✕Try to avoidEight similar angles can't be ranked by eye.
✓RecommendedA sorted bar ranks them instantly.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals12

Fundamentals

People data is personal

Workforce charts describe colleagues, and carry extra obligations.

Minimum group size

No group under 10 people: not in bars, labels, tooltips, filters or drill-downs. Merge into "Other" and footnote it.

No re-identification

Small team × tenure × location can single out one person, even when each cut is large.

Protected attributes and forecasts

Protected attributes only for approved analyses such as pay equity, aggregated. Label estimates and show a range. Frame findings about roles, not individuals.

Engagement by team, one distribution center

Two teams have fewer than 10 respondents: anyone who knows the team can guess who answered what.

TeamRespondentsEngagement
Inbound4671
Outbound3868
Returns752
Quality488
Site leadership981
✕Try to avoidReporting groups below the minimum, even in a table or tooltip.

Engagement by team, one distribution center

Small teams combined into one group that clears the threshold.

TeamRespondentsEngagement
Inbound4671
Outbound3868
Other teams (3 combined)2072
✓RecommendedMerge into "Other" and footnote it: "Teams with fewer than 10 respondents are combined."

In dashboards, enforce it in the data model

A rule in a slide is easy to forget; a rule in the measure can't be skipped. In Power BI: IF([Headcount] < 10, BLANK(), [Engagement]). In Python, drop or merge small groups before plotting, and keep individual values out of hover text.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals13

Fundamentals

Accessible by default

About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have a color-vision deficiency. In a room of 25, assume someone does.

  • Text contrast at least 4.5:1
  • Never red vs. green; use blues and navy, with orange only for "worse"
  • Never color alone: pair it with labels, position or shape
  • Nothing below 9 pt on slides or 11 px on screens
  • Alt text for every chart that leaves the team: the headline plus two or three key numbers

The red–green examples are simulated for deuteranopia, the most common form.

Red vs. green

✕As seen with deuteranopiaRed and green hires vs. exits become one color.
✓As seen with deuteranopiaBlue and light blue stay distinct.

Color as the only cue

✕Try to avoidThe reader matches colors to a legend.
✓RecommendedNames at the line ends; color only reinforces.

Text on fills

✕Try to avoidWhite on every fill fails on the light ones.
✓RecommendedWhite or navy, whichever contrasts more.

Alt text

Write it from the headline and the numbers that prove it.

Alt: Two frontline job families lose about 1 in 4 people a year, well above the 19.9% enterprise rate. Pharmacy Technician 27.4%; Distribution Center Associate 24.1%; all other job families are below the enterprise rate.

In PowerPoint: right-click the chart, View Alt Text. In HTML: aria-label on the figure.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals14

Magnitude

Bar chart

Magnitude charts compare size: which is bigger (relative), and by how much (absolute).

A bar's length is proportional to its value, so bars are the most precise way to compare categories. Sorted horizontal bars are the default for ranking job families, sites or skills: long names stay readable, and the layout works on a phone.

Use columns for a few time periods or short names.

McKesson spec

  • Bar about 2× the gap (Excel gap width 50%)
  • Sorted by value unless there's a natural order
  • Up to about 12 bars; group the tail into "Other"
  • No group under 10 people
  1. 1Insight headlineNames the two families and the benchmark they beat.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, unit, scope, period.
  3. 3Focus in blueOnly the bars the headline names; two at most.
  4. 4Echo in the labelFocus categories in bold navy.
  5. 5Values on the barsSo the value axis and gridlines go.
  6. 6Labelled benchmarkA thin dashed line, named where it sits.
  7. 7Zero baselineA thin axis line; bars always start at zero.
  8. 8Grey contextEverything else, sorted by value.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceDefines the metric; names system, date, population.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude15

Magnitude

Bar chart variants

Same rules, different shapes. Pick the variant from the comparison you need to make.

When a bar is the wrong chart

  • Values bunched far from zero (engagement 71–78): use a dot plot
  • Largest more than 20× the smallest: use proportional bubbles or split the chart
  • Parts of a whole: use a 100% stacked bar or waterfall
  • Many periods: use a line
  • Spread across people: use a distribution

Column chart

A few periods in time order, or short category names. Here internal fill rose from 22% to 29%.

Grouped bars

Two or three series per category. Prior period in light grey, current in blue; key top-left.

Diverging bars

Values on both sides of zero. Three job families shrank in FY26 despite hiring; negatives in orange.

Butterfly chart

Two measures back to back on the same items: FY26 exits and hires by job family.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude16

Magnitude

Bar chart best practice

Four rules that fix most bar charts.

Size of bars. Thin bars pull the eye to the empty space between them. Make each bar about twice as wide as the gap.

Color of bars. A different color per bar distracts and implies categories that don't exist. One color; shade only the highlight.

Direct labels. Gridlines and a value axis add noise. Label the bars and delete both.

Zero baseline. Bar length encodes quantity, so never truncate. If the data needs a narrow range, switch to a line or dot plot.

Size of bars

✕Try to avoidStick-thin bars; the gaps dominate.
✓RecommendedBar about twice the gap.

Color of bars

✕Try to avoidA color per bar, encoding nothing.
✓RecommendedGrey bars; blue for the one that matters.

Direct labels

✕Try to avoidGridlines and an axis to read values from.
✓RecommendedValues on the bars; no axis, no grid.

Zero baseline

✕Try to avoidA truncated axis exaggerates differences.
✓RecommendedA line or dot plot can use a narrow range.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude17

Magnitude

Bar chart best practice, continued

Four more, from reviewing workforce decks.

Sort with intent. Alphabetical order hides the ranking. Sort by value unless the categories have a natural order: tenure bands, job levels, survey scales.

Horizontal for long names. Rotated labels are slow to read. Job-family names need horizontal bars.

Label the benchmark in place. A reference line explained in a legend makes the reader search. Name it on the line.

Two highlights at most. Five colored bars in two colors is decoration, not emphasis.

Sort with intent

✕Try to avoidAlphabetical: the ranking is hidden.
✓RecommendedBy value, largest on top.

Horizontal for long names

✕Try to avoidTilted names the reader has to decode.
✓RecommendedHorizontal bars; names read naturally.

Label the benchmark

✕Try to avoidA legend for one line, in a highlight color.
✓RecommendedNavy dashed line, named on the line.

Two highlights at most

✕Try to avoidEverything highlighted means nothing is.
✓RecommendedThe two the headline names.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude18

Magnitude

Build a bar chart

The same chart in every tool we use. Each recipe starts from the starter kit, so the colors and fonts are already right.

Full, tested code for each platform is on the cookbook page: docs/cookbook/bar.md.

Before you send it

  • Starts at zero; bar about 2× the gap
  • Sorted by value or a natural order
  • Values labelled; no value axis or gridlines
  • At most two highlights, matching the headline
  • Benchmark labelled in place
  • No group under 10 people
PowerPoint and Excel

Start from the starter deck or chart workbook in dist/office/. Insert a clustered bar, sort the data ascending (so the largest is on top), set Gap Width 50%, fill all bars with Context grey and the focus bars with Focus blue. Add data labels at Outside End; delete the value axis, gridlines, legend and chart title. The slide title is the headline.

Power BI

Import mckesson-dataviz-theme.json and sort the bars by the measure. Drive the highlight from a measure, not by clicking bars: a Bar color measure returns the focus blue when attrition is above 20% and context grey otherwise, applied through Colors › fx › Field value. Turn on data labels; turn off the X axis and gridlines. See docs/powerbi-setup.md.

Python

matplotlib with mckviz; Plotly uses the same helpers (mv.pl_highlight).

bars = ax.barh(df.job_family, df.rate, height=0.67,
               color=mv.highlight(df.job_family, focus=focus))
mv.label_bars(ax, bars, fmt="{:.1f}%")
mv.clean_axes(ax, keep=("left",), grid=None); ax.set_xticks([])
mv.titles(fig, headline, subtitle); mv.source(fig, source)
mv.lint(fig)   # checks colors, zero baseline, labels vs. axis
HTML

Copy templates/html/chart-card.html: headline, subtitle and source are HTML, colors come from CSS variables such as var(--mck-chart-focus), and the chart is drawn after the font loads.

R

source("dist/r/theme_mck.R"), then geom_col(aes(fill = job_family), width = 0.67) + scale_fill_manual(values = mck_highlight(levels(df$job_family), focus = focus), guide = "none") + theme_mck().

Coding agents

"Make a McKesson bar chart of voluntary attrition by job family, FY26, highlighting the families above the enterprise rate." The mck-chart skill runs the workflow and returns the chart, a chart brief and alt text.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude19

Part-to-whole

Stacked bar chart

Part-to-whole charts show how a whole breaks into its parts, and how each part relates to the total.

A 100% stacked bar compares the mix of several wholes at once. Color only the segment the headline is about, and put it on the baseline or at the end of each bar.

McKesson spec

  • Five segments at most; group the rest as "Other"
  • White separators between segments
  • Labels inside segments that fit; key top-left in stack order
  • Sort the bars by the segment that matters
  1. 1Insight headlineNames the part and how far it stands out.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, unit, scope, period.
  3. 3The part that mattersOne segment in blue, at the end of every bar.
  4. 4Grey contextTwo greys for the other parts.
  5. 5Labels in the segmentsWhere they fit; navy on grey, white on blue.
  6. 6Key in stack orderTop-left, left to right as the segments run.
  7. 7Echo the valueThe story segment's value at the bar end, bold for the focus bar.
  8. 8Sorted by the storyBars ordered by the blue segment, not alphabetically.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceDefine the parts.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole20

Part-to-whole

Stacked bar variants

Same rules: one part in color, the rest grey, labels in place.

When a stack is the wrong chart

  • One whole with up to five parts: a donut or a single bar
  • How a total changes step by step: a waterfall
  • Many parts or a hierarchy: a treemap
  • Comparing the parts themselves across groups: grouped bars or small multiples; only the baseline segment of a stack compares cleanly

Stacked columns with totals

When the total matters too. The FY30 Data & AI gap of 617 FTE: reskilling (on the baseline) closes 40%.

Diverging stacked bars

Survey scales. Unfavorable in orange left of zero (it means worse), favorable in blue, neutral split across the middle.

Marimekko

Width and height both carry data: column width is each function's workforce, height its mix. Powerful, but it needs explaining.

Mix over time

A few periods as 100% columns, the tracked segment on the baseline so its change reads directly.

McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole21

Part-to-whole

Stacked bar best practice

Stacks are easy to make and easy to misread. Four rules keep them honest.

The part that matters on the baseline. Only segments that share a starting line can be compared by eye.

Five segments at most. More slices turn a bar into a barcode. Keep the parts the story needs and group the rest.

Label in place; key in stack order. If a key is needed, put it top-left, in the same order as the segments.

One order in every bar. Never re-sort segments within each bar.

The part that matters on the baseline

✕Try to avoidA floating segment can't be compared across bars.
✓RecommendedOn the baseline, every bar starts level.

Five segments at most

✕Try to avoidEight colored slices nobody can follow.
✓RecommendedThe part in blue, the rest in grey.

Label in place, key in order

✕Try to avoidA bottom legend in a different order.
✓RecommendedValues inside, key top-left in stack order.

One order in every bar

✕Try to avoidSegments re-sorted inside each bar.
✓RecommendedThe same order everywhere.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole22

Part-to-whole

Waterfall chart

A waterfall shows how a starting total becomes an ending total, one driver at a time.

It is a stacked column chart with an invisible spacer series that floats each driver at the running total. Use it for labor cost bridges, headcount bridges and budget-to-actual walks.

McKesson spec

  • Totals in navy; drivers grey; the drivers the headline names in blue
  • Thin light connectors between bars
  • Signed labels on drivers (true minus, explicit +); bold totals
  • If the axis starts above zero, mark the break and say so
  1. 1Insight headlineSizes what the named drivers did to the total.
  2. 2SubtitleFrom and to, with the unit.
  3. 3Totals in navyStart, end and any subtotal.
  4. 4Marked breakThe axis starts at $3,900M; white slashes say so.
  5. 5The drivers that matterIn blue; label bold.
  6. 6Thin connectorsLight grey, so the bars stay dominant.
  7. 7Signed labels+139, −58: direction without color.
  8. 8Grey contextEvery other driver, in logical order.
  9. 9FootnoteStates the axis break.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole23

Part-to-whole

Waterfall variants

The same build, turned or recolored for the job.

Color by direction only when direction is the point. In a headcount bridge, additions in blue and losses in orange read instantly, because orange means "worse". In a cost bridge the default stays grey with a blue highlight.

Excel's built-in Waterfall chart is vertical only. For horizontal waterfalls or per-bar colors, build a stacked bar with a transparent spacer series (see the cookbook).

Horizontal waterfall

Long driver names, narrow layouts and phones.

Colored by direction

Frontline headcount bridge: voluntary exits equal 97% of external hires.

With a subtotal

A light-blue subtotal separates cost growth from the savings that offset it.

Distribution waterfall

Contributions to one total instead of steps in time: data engineering is 34% of the FY30 gap.

McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole24

Part-to-whole

Waterfall best practice

The bars carry the story; everything else stays quiet.

Thin connectors. Heavy dark connectors compete with the bars. Use hairlines in light grey.

No red and green. They fail for color-blind readers and aren't McKesson colors. Grey drivers with a blue highlight, or blue and orange when direction is the story.

Mark a broken axis. Totals often dwarf the drivers. Starting the axis above zero is allowed here, and only here, if the break is drawn and footnoted.

Group the small steps. Keep the drivers the story needs; fold the rest together.

Connector lines

✕Try to avoidHeavy, dark connectors.
✓RecommendedThin, light grey.

Coloring the bars

✕Try to avoidGreen up, red down.
✓RecommendedGrey drivers; the named ones blue.

A broken axis

✕Try to avoidCut totals with no warning.
✓RecommendedBreak marks and a note.

Group the small steps

✕Try to avoidTen narrow drivers to decode.
✓RecommendedFive steps, savings combined.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole25

Part-to-whole

Treemap

Nested rectangles whose area is proportional to value. A treemap shows many parts, or a hierarchy, in one compact block.

Use it when there are too many parts for a donut or a stack (ten to thirty roles, sites or skills) and the point is which few dominate.

Don't use it when readers need to compare similar sizes precisely, or there are only a handful of parts: a sorted bar is clearer.

McKesson spec

  • Squarified layout, largest top-left
  • Thin, even white gutters
  • Grey tiles; the ones the headline names in blue
  • Name and value inside each tile that fits
  1. 1Insight headlineShare of the whole held by the named few.
  2. 2SubtitleWhat area measures, with the unit.
  3. 3Focus in blueThe two roles the headline names.
  4. 4Grey contextEvery other role, the same grey.
  5. 5Smallest lastBottom-right. Tiles too small for a label get none; list them in a footnote if they matter.
  6. 6Largest firstTop-left, flowing to the smallest; labels top-left inside each tile.
  7. 7Footnote and sourceDefine the measure.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole26

Part-to-whole

Treemap best practice

A treemap works when it reads as one shape that flows from large to small.

Largest to smallest. Don't arrange tiles alphabetically or by an org grouping that breaks the flow.

Labels inside. No label bands or boxes over the tiles; they distort the areas. If a tile can't hold its label, leave it unlabelled or label it outside.

Even padding. Uneven gaps make similar tiles look different.

Few parts? Use a bar. Areas are harder to compare than lengths.

Arrange by size

✕Try to avoidAlphabetical strips.
✓RecommendedLargest top-left.

Labelling

✕Try to avoidLabel bands over the tiles.
✓RecommendedInside, top-left.

Padding

✕Try to avoidUneven gaps.
✓RecommendedThin, even gutters.

Few parts

✕Try to avoidFour similar tiles.
✓RecommendedA sorted bar ranks them.

Part-to-whole

Donut and pie

A donut shows one whole split into a few parts. Prefer it to a pie: readers follow the arc length around the ring, and the center holds the total.

Use it for one whole and at most five parts. To compare several wholes, use 100% stacked bars; for more parts, a bar or treemap.

McKesson spec

  • Five segments at most; "Other" last
  • Largest first, clockwise from 12 o'clock
  • Hole about 60% of the diameter; white separators
  • Labels and values outside; no legend
  1. 1Insight headlineThe share, and what it means for the plan.
  2. 2SubtitleThe whole, the unit, the year.
  3. 3Start at 12Largest first, then clockwise.
  4. 4The part that mattersIn blue; the rest grey.
  5. 5Total in the centerLight weight, large.
  6. 6Labels outsideName and share, beside each segment.
  7. 7White separatorsThin gaps keep segments distinct.
  8. 8Footnote and sourceDefine the parts.

Part-to-whole

Donut best practice

People judge length faster than angle or area, which is why the donut beats the pie.

Donut over pie. The ring turns angles into arc lengths, and the hole holds the total.

Labels outside. Squeezed labels on the ring are hard to read; put names and values outside.

Few segments. Group the smallest into "Other".

Largest first, clockwise from 12. Don't mix small and large at random.

Progress rings and dials for a single percentage are in Single number.

Donut over pie

✕Try to avoidAngles and areas.
✓RecommendedArc lengths on a ring.

Labelling

✕Try to avoidLabels squeezed onto the ring.
✓RecommendedOutside, with the share.

Many small segments

✕Try to avoidNine slices, nine colors.
✓RecommendedThe story, plus "Other".

Order of segments

✕Try to avoidNo order, odd start.
✓RecommendedLargest first from 12.

Part-to-whole

Build part-to-whole charts

Every tool can make these natively. The settings below are the ones that matter; tested code and click-by-click steps are on the cookbook pages.

stacked-bar.md · waterfall.md · treemap.md · donut-pie.md

Before you send it

  • Parts sum to the whole (100%, or the end total)
  • Five parts at most; "Other" last
  • One part in color, matching the headline
  • Waterfall axis break marked and footnoted
  • No group under 10 people, in any part
PowerPoint and Excel

Stacked: Stacked or 100% Stacked Bar, Gap Width 50%, Overlap 100%, white 1.5 pt borders; move the story series first or last in Select Data. Waterfall: Insert › Waterfall, then right-click each total › Set as Total; drivers grey, totals navy. Treemap: Insert › Hierarchy › Treemap; labels Overlapping, not Banner. Donut: Doughnut, angle of first slice 0°, hole 62%, data sorted descending.

Power BI

Native 100% stacked bar, Waterfall, Treemap and Donut visuals all take the theme. Set the story color per series or with a field-value color measure; legend top-left or off; data labels on. The native waterfall can't color single bars or break the axis: use a stacked column with a transparent spacer measure when you need that.

Python

ax.barh(..., left=running_total, edgecolor="white") for stacks; the waterfall, squarified treemap and donut recipes in the cookbook use only matplotlib and mckviz. Plotly has native go.Waterfall, go.Treemap and go.Pie(hole=0.6).

colors = mv.highlight(parts, focus="Contingent")          # one part blue, rest grey
mv.lint(fig)    # flags > 6 colors, legends, and bars that don't start at zero
HTML

Plotly with MCK_PLOTLY_TEMPLATE: barmode: "stack", waterfall and treemap traces. Read colors from var(--mck-chart-focus) and var(--mck-chart-context).

R

geom_col(position = "fill") for 100% stacks; treemapify::geom_treemap() for treemaps; waterfalls with geom_rect(). Colors from mck_highlight().
